analysis.one_liner: Requires new keyless-ignition cars to shut off automatically to prevent carbon monoxide poisoning and rollaway crashes.
analysis.headline: Introduced with one cosponsor in April 2021, the bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Transportation Department to finish safety rules for cars with keyless ignitions. New cars would need to shut off automatically after idling long enough to cause carbon monoxide poisoning, and to lock in place so they cannot roll away when parked unsafely. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, passengers, and households would benefit from two vehicle safety protections: cars with keyless ignitions that automatically shut off after idling long enough to risk carbon monoxide poisoning, and technology that prevents a parked car from rolling away when the driver's door is open, the seat belt is unbuckled, and the brake is not engaged [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill orders the Transportation Department to finalize a rule requiring automatic shutoff technology in keyless-ignition, internal-combustion vehicles, so a car left running in an enclosed space shuts off before it can poison people nearby with carbon monoxide

It orders a second rule requiring technology that keeps a vehicle with an automatic transmission from rolling away when it is not in park, the driver's door is open, the seat belt is unbuckled, and the brake is not engaged
It sets a deadline: the rules must be issued within two years of enactment and take effect the following September 1, closing off the indefinite delays that had kept related rulemaking open

analysis.who_pays: Automakers would pay to design and install the shutoff and anti-rollaway technology, and those costs would likely be passed into new-vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies only to new vehicles; the millions of keyless-ignition cars already on the road would remain unaffected, so the safety gains arrive only gradually
Compliance costs fall on manufacturers and would likely be passed along to buyers in new-vehicle prices, at a time when car prices were already rising

The bill delegates key safety details — the idle time before shutoff and the maximum rollaway speed — to the Transportation Secretary to determine, so the real-world strength of the rules would depend on the agency's judgment

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are targeted and concrete: carbon monoxide poisoning from vehicles left running in garages and rollaway crashes are recurring, preventable deaths, and the technology to prevent both already exists on many models. The costs are modest per-vehicle compliance expenses that would show up slightly in new-car prices, though only new cars benefit and the rules' strength would rest on the Secretary's judgment. On balance the bill is a reasonable, low-cost safety mandate, but its narrow scope limits how much good it could do.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Commerce Committee after its referral and never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the PARK IT Act on April 21, 2021, with Senator Markey as its sole cosponsor
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, the only committee action it received
No hearing, markup, or vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers are better off because the bill died: no federal mandate was created requiring automatic shutoff and anti-rollaway technology on keyless-ignition vehicles.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Car makers avoided the safety mandate

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it as its Senate sponsor

for.name: Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only senator to do so

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (Chair Maria Cantwell)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote; its only recorded support came from two Democratic senators, and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would require automakers to design and install automatic shutoff and anti-rollaway technology in new keyless-ignition vehicles, a compliance cost. Auto manufacturers have historically resisted mandated safety equipment, and no automaker publicly supported the bill.
